source: As I brought everyone together for the announcement this morning, one of my men reported back from Fortinbras's cell.
The Prince has escaped.
Lady Birgitta is missing as well.
(So I witnessed.)
What happened? How could he escape?
I believe his men watched for any sign of chaos within our ranks to come forth.
That moment of congregation was the only moment they needed.
So if someone dies... I see, now.
Surely, the Prince's forthcoming assault will be delayed, but—not spurned, as we'd hoped.
I'm rallying my men now. I'm certain we will still prevail.
(I had everything lined up! It seems fixing our external affairs means little, if internal affairs are still bloody.)
It is truly a detestable situation.
(There has to be a way to keep them all alive.)
I'm aware of the situation, Bernardo. Please—do your best.
(It won't matter regardless.)
I must inform the others. I'm sorry I could not do more.
(Hopefully, this at least bought me enough time to meet Simona.)
Everyone, out of the bar. Immediately.
In the name of Norway, submit!
If you flee, you'll be killed!
It's time. Begin the siege.
And what have we here...?
Who are you, dressed in fine clothing?
...Ah. Dark little noblewoman. I've heard of you: Lord Polonius's daughter.
Headed up to the castle to tell the King about our siege, it would seem.
My lady, the old ways are over. Your family means nothing now. The reign of Norway begins today.
Submit to me, and there is no need for useless bloodshed. I do not wish your life.
If you're waiting for fear or deference, I'll show you neither.
You're attacking my home and my family. If you so eschew violence, what's all this?
I did not come here for debate. I came to take action against a tyrant. If you would defend him, so be it. Men, keep her in our custody. Indefinitely.
The invasion marches onward.

source: We're here to rescue our Prince from you louts!
And we won't stop until every wall is rubble.
(I can't stay here. If they capture me, they'll use me as ransom.)
Fortinbras's capture was an insult to Norway, but now that he's returned, we'll return the action tenfold!
Men, something unusual has happened today in capturing Prince Fortinbras.
This may seem advantageous to us, but I anticipate it is only an omen of more to come.
All of you are to be on highest guard over the next few days.
Any sign of suspicious activity—any outbreaks of violence in town—relay them to me personally.
Do you all understand?
A' course, Cap'n.
Good. Dismissed.
Lady Ophelia—please come wiv' me.
The King's requested everyone gather in the Great Hall.
No need to be alarmed, everyone.
E-everything's quite under control.
(He doesn't look confident.)
I've ordered you all here for your own protection.
Right now, all remaining men, including Bernardo, are fortifying our outer walls against Norway's attacks.
As we have Prince Fortinbras now, they've agreed to a temporary truce. But in all likelihood, it shall not last.
I've sent word to the nobility to commit themselves to me and send reinforcements posthaste.
No matter what, this central tower is strong. It has withstood many an invasion throughout its history.
Indeed, it is the only section that remained when Elsinore was last reduced to rubble.
You mean we're all meant to sequester here?
For the time being, yes. Everyone must remain here.
Make yourselves comfortable. If need be, the kitchen is stocked and the fire is stoked.
There is an adjacent chamber with servants' quarters as well. It is meager, but sufficient.
We shan't be here longer than a day if our allies respond as they ought.
Nothin' to fear, folks! I'll be keepin yeh all safe in the meantime.
How long do you think this will go on, Horatio?
Hard to say.
Now the true war begins.
This will not be easily finished.
I'll be the first to say it, Ophelia. I am afraid.
Of what?
Not of death. I have seen battle many a time.
But of... the war.
Some wars are over swiftly. The fight is won, one side destroys another, and all rebuild.
But some wars... are wasting wars.
When men whittle each other to the bone, refusing to acknowledge a victor, yet failing to force the other to defeat...
It's hell on a country. Everyone loses in a wasting war.
But we have Prince Fortinbras in jail. We could win, couldn't we? If the reinforcements arrive?
Those, too, will be meager.
Claudius was dismissive of the nobility. They will be hesitant to lend him their men. Some may have outright allied with Fortinbras.
And even with the Prince in jail, they will not yield to Claudius.
Many are quietly praying for a coup, and a new election to the throne...
But we're still alive.
Isn't that what matters? We survived. We lived on.
It's certainly a perk.
And when the war is over, something will remain, one way or another.
We'll build a new Denmark. We'll raise new walls. We'll patch the holes.
Well, then. I daresay you are far too chipper at the moment.
Where is the wine? Surely there's some in the kitchen, right?
If we're all going right into the mouth of Hell, might as well be drunk when we arrive.
Hear, hear.
Don't wander too far.
(I could use the Book of Fates to keep this world forever.)
(This world is collapsing now. I feel it.)
Carried back again.

source: (...I still don't know what keeps me trapped here.)
(Until then, I can never see what lies beyond the horizon of this world.)
Good morning, Horatio.
Are you well this morning?
Of course. Always up for a walk to lift the spirits!
You are the only man who will take me for a stroll these days, Horatio.
It's as though half the time these days my husband is concealed away in his chambers, lost in thought.
My husband would have gone on these strolls with me, once.
Even if my husband were available to do it, I don't know that I'd care to walk with him much. Not now, at least.
My Queen, these walks are a treat. Your beauty is so great that when people see us out, I look handsome just standing next to you.
Heh. You flatter me.
Say, Horatio...
I know nothing about you. Have you ever told me of yourself?
My late husband often spoke of your prowess on the battlefield. But what before that?
There's not much to tell, my lady. I'm but a poor footsoldier. Then I followed Hamlet to Wittenberg, for a time.
I didn't care much for the area, I'm afraid. No offense to your Bohemian heritage.
No offense taken. I consider myself Danish now. But where were you born?
Italy, your Highness.
Italy! What! So far from here? What is it like?
Italy is... hard to describe. Loud and hot, and at once, brimming with quiet beauty.
My father was a spice merchant in Venice, originally of Calicut. He sailed the route and took me with him often, when I was a boy. It was in Calicut he met my mother.
But their love was brief, her pregnancy was a secret, and they were unwed. After I was born, my father absconded with me to Venice to save her reputation.
How sad for your mother, don't you think?
I wouldn't know. I saw her just once or twice when I was a boy. She was married off to another man. After that, Father and I never saw her again.
But my father loved me dearly.
What of your life after that? Venice, India, Denmark—you've traveled perpetually.
Why, my lady, my secrets are the key to my charm!
It's just a lot of nothing anyhow. I far prefer my life these days. Venice holds certain painful memories for me.
I'm sorry to hear that. Well, regardless, I'm glad you're here.
As am I.
I must go. Same time tomorrow?
Of course, Your Highness.
My lady, shall we stroll?
Of course!
Yesterday I spilled all my secrets to you, my Queen. Are you going to return the favor?
Hmm. You want to know about me?
Is that so surprising?
N-no, it's just... I've never been asked before. Hmm, where to begin...
When I was a girl in Bohemia, my father the Emperor once told me I would be one of the most powerful women in the world.
And he was right. He sent me here to Denmark when I was just a girl. I grew up here, between Copenhagen and Elsinore, betrothed to Hamlet's father.
I followed Hamlet everywhere. He was all I knew, for a time. The only friend I had. He, and Claudius, his brother, and my elder sister Margaret.
My elder sister Margaret stayed behind in Austria. She's very powerful now, with land all to her own, and armies at her beckon...
I suppose this is... all a very different life from the one you've lived. I hope I'm not offending.
On the contrary, I find it very interesting.
What became of your sister Margaret? Do you speak to her still?
Margaret was everything to me when we were young. I loved her more than life itself.
When I came to Elsinore... I wrote her letters every day. And she wrote back, sometimes.
But it was always to encourage me to cease contact, to study more, to love my new country and forget Austria entirely.
Eventually, she stopped responding entirely. And I haven't seen her since.
I missed her. I still dream of her sometimes—of us, playing as children again.
I'm so sorry, my lady.
How perfectly awful. I've never had siblings, but I can imagine.
It is no matter. All the love I had for Margaret, I have poured into my husband and son. I hope they have appreciated it.
Apologies, but I must go.
Understood. See you tomorrrow.
Ah, my lady... fresh as a rose.
You flatterer. Shall we stroll?
So. My Queen. I find myself poring over an interesting dilemma.
Oh? Do you, now?
What is to become of Hamlet now?
Are you to quietly betroth him somewhere, given all that's happened?
Send him away into some new life?
Not with the predicament he's in.
Yes. You see, your son is a fascinating creature in a fascinating position. High-born, yet utterly unsurrounded by ladies of his equivalence.
My husband and I have both noticed this problem.
Is that why he remains unbetrothed to any woman?
That, among other... problems. I don't know that I'd be able to make a suitable match with the state he's in.
His mind's all strange at the moment.
He's killed a man. No court will want him. He shall be an outlaw in reputation, if not in name. I fear for his immediate future.
Horatio, what will I do? I just...
